Name: counterfactual_biophysics_probe
Title: Do Protein Language Models Represent Causal Biophysical Mechanisms or Just Evolutionary Correlations? A Counterfactual Mutational Test
Short Hypothesis: If a protein language model's internal features encode genuine biophysical mechanisms (e.g., hydrophobicity-driven core packing, charge complementarity at salt bridges, disulfide bonding geometry), then targeted point mutations that physically break a mechanism will causally deactivate the corresponding internal feature in a manner predicted by the physics, whereas mutations that only alter evolutionary conservation but preserve the mechanism will not. Distinguishing mechanistic from merely correlational representations is the key open question left by existing annotation-matching interpretability work. We define a 'mechanistic' feature operationally and narrowly as one whose activation changes monotonically with a specified physical parameter (e.g., hydrophobicity change, Coulombic energy) under these interventions, not merely one that co-occurs with an annotation.
Related Work: A rapidly growing body of work (InterPLM, ProtSAE, Matryoshka SAEs on ESM2-3B, Automated Neuron Labelling, ProtoMech circuit tracing, and the 2026 review 'What Do Biological Foundation Models Compute?') applies sparse autoencoders and probes to protein language models and finds features matching known annotations (binding sites, secondary structure, GO terms). Crucially, that review explicitly identifies a 'critical gap': validation relies almost exclusively on matching features against existing annotations, risking circularity because those annotations derive from the same evolutionary sequences the model was trained on. Zhang et al. (categorical Jacobian) showed ESM-2 stores coevolutionary statistics like a Markov Random Field, hinting that some 'structural' knowledge is actually correlational. No prior work causally tests whether recovered features track the underlying *physical mechanism* versus evolutionary co-occurrence. This also differs from activation-steering and causal-tracing studies, which establish that a feature is *used* by the model but not whether it tracks a *physically valid* mechanism; our counterfactuals are anchored to external biophysical ground truth rather than to the model's own downstream behavior. Our proposal directly closes this gap with a counterfactual, physics-grounded intervention protocol rather than more annotation matching.
Abstract: Foundation models of protein sequence encode features that correlate with known biological concepts, but a fundamental ambiguity remains: do these features represent the causal biophysical mechanisms underlying structure and function, or merely the evolutionary statistics that happen to accompany them? Because the annotations used to validate interpretability are themselves derived from evolutionary data, existing evidence cannot separate the two. We propose a counterfactual mutational framework to resolve this. We first identify interpretable features (via sparse autoencoders and linear probes on ESM-2) that align with three physically well-understood mechanisms: hydrophobic core packing, salt-bridge electrostatics, and disulfide bonding. We then design paired in-silico mutations: (1) mechanism-breaking mutations that physically abolish the interaction (e.g., mutating a buried hydrophobic residue to a charged one, neutralizing a salt-bridge partner, or removing one cysteine of a disulfide pair), and (2) mechanism-preserving control mutations that change conservation/evolutionary signal by comparable amounts but keep the physical mechanism intact (e.g., conservative hydrophobic-to-hydrophobic substitutions, or charge-swapping both partners of a salt bridge to preserve complementarity). If features are mechanistic, feature activation should drop specifically for mechanism-breaking mutations and follow quantitative physical predictions (e.g., magnitude scaling with hydrophobicity change or Coulombic energy). We quantify mechanism-selectivity, dose-response to physical parameters, and agreement with molecular-mechanics energy estimates. This yields a systematic causal, physics-grounded test of whether biological foundation models learn mechanisms or correlations. The contributions are, explicitly: a counterfactual intervention *protocol*, a *finding* about whether representations are mechanistic or merely correlational, and physics-grounded *controls* against evolutionary-statistics explanations. If the test is negative, practitioners in variant-effect prediction and protein design should treat feature-level mechanistic interpretations as unproven and use them only with external biophysical validation; if positive, internal features become materially more trustworthy design handles. Either way the result raises the evidentiary bar for interpretability claims in protein ML and speaks to structural biology and protein/drug engineering, not only interpretability researchers.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Mechanism-feature identification and baseline correspondence): Tests the H1 sub-claim that ESM-2 residue activations carry identifiable features corresponding to three biophysical mechanisms (buried hydrophobic core packing, salt-bridge charge complementarity, disulfide geometry). Data: high-resolution X-ray structures from the PDB (~200k structures with resolution <2.0 Å exist); we use a PISCES-culled non-redundant set of 1,000 chains (≤25% pairwise sequence identity, resolution <2.0 Å, R-free <0.25), split 600 train / 200 validation / 200 test by chain — 1,000 is chosen because it yields ~250k labeled residues, enough to fit probes/SAEs, while the identity cull prevents homolog leakage; more chains add compute without new mechanism types. Ground-truth per-residue labels from DSSP + Reduce: buried hydrophobic (relative solvent accessibility <0.1 AND residue in {Leu,Ile,Val,Phe,Met}), salt bridge (oppositely-charged side-chain N/O atoms within 4.0 Å), disulfide (S–S <2.5 Å). Model: ESM-2 150M and 650M, backbone frozen; trainable = per-layer sparse autoencoders (dictionary size 8,192, L1 penalty 1e-3, Adam lr 1e-3, 100 epochs) and L2-logistic linear probes, fit on activations from every 6th layer; 3 seeds. Systems compared: SAE top-feature vs supervised linear probe vs matched-norm random-direction control. Decisive metric first: held-out test AUROC of the best probe and F1 of the best-matching SAE feature, per mechanism. Convincing result: AUROC ≥ 0.90 with one identifiable feature/direction per mechanism at some layer. Undecidable band: AUROC in [0.70, 0.80] — a mechanism whose best readout lands here is too weakly localized for a clean causal test, so it is reported as inconclusive and dropped from Experiments 2–4; this band call is fixed before running. Negative result: all three mechanisms below 0.70 AUROC means ESM-2 carries no identifiable mechanism feature, H1 fails, and H2/H3 are moot.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Counterfactual mechanism-breaking vs conservation-matched-preserving causal test): Tests the H2 sub-claim that mutations physically breaking a mechanism deactivate its feature while mutations that shift only evolutionary conservation but preserve the mechanism do not. Data: from the 200 test chains of Experiment 1, curate 300 proteins carrying at least one clean instance of each mechanism (300 chosen to give ~100 paired sites per mechanism at 3 seeds, feasible on one GPU; fewer would underpower the paired test). For each site build three in-silico single/double point mutations: (i) mechanism-breaking (buried Leu/Ile/Val/Phe→Asp/Lys; charge removal of one salt-bridge partner; Cys→Ser removing one disulfide partner), (ii) mechanism-preserving physical control (hydrophobic→similar-volume hydrophobic; simultaneous Asp–Lys→Lys–Asp swap keeping complementarity), (iii) conservation-matched control whose BLOSUM62/PSSM conservation change equals the breaking mutation's but leaves the physical mechanism intact, and (iv) a generic-perturbation null: random substitutions matched only on amino-acid class and local sequence context, estimating baseline feature sensitivity to any mutation (a mechanistic feature must move more for breaking mutations than for this null). Power: ~100 paired sites per mechanism give >0.8 power to detect a paired effect size of 0.3 (Wilcoxon signed-rank, alpha 0.05). Model: same frozen ESM-2 150M/650M and the fixed Experiment-1 feature directions; no new training; 3 seeds over mutation sampling. Systems compared: Δ feature activation at the mutated residue and its partner for breaking vs physical-preserving vs conservation-matched. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity index S = |Δ_break| / |Δ_preserve| (paired across sites, Wilcoxon signed-rank). Convincing result: S significantly > 1 for all tested mechanisms AND breaking > conservation-matched (showing the effect is physical, not conservation-driven). Undecidable band: S in [0.9, 1.3] — a mechanism landing here shows no reliable break-vs-preserve separation, read as "feature is correlational for that mechanism" (H2 not supported there); band fixed before data. Negative result: S ≈ 1 across mechanisms, or breaking indistinguishable from conservation-matched, means the features are correlational rather than mechanistic and H2 fails.

Experiment 3 (H3 — Physics dose-response and molecular-mechanics agreement): Tests the H3 sub-claim that feature deactivation is quantitatively predicted by the physics, not merely present. Data: the same 300 proteins / paired mutations from Experiment 2, plus per-mutation physical quantities computed once: Kyte–Doolittle hydrophobicity change and buried-surface-area change (hydrophobic), Coulombic interaction energy from geometry (salt bridge), and a geometric bonding indicator (disulfide); plus FoldX ΔΔG (single point-mutation ΔΔG, 5 FoldX runs averaged) for every mutation. Model: frozen ESM-2 650M with fixed Experiment-1 directions; no training. Systems compared: correlation of Δ feature activation with the physical quantity for mechanism-breaking mutations vs conservation-matched controls. Decisive metric first: Spearman ρ between Δ activation and the physical driver (per mechanism), and ΔR² of feature change in predicting FoldX ΔΔG for breaking vs conservation-matched mutations. Convincing result: monotone dose-response ρ ≥ 0.5 for breaking mutations AND feature change predicts ΔΔG significantly better for breaking than conservation-matched (ΔR² > 0). Undecidable band: |ρ| in [0.2, 0.35] — weak, physics-consistent-but-not-decisive coupling; a mechanism here is reported as "partially mechanistic" and not counted as H3 support; band fixed in advance. Negative result: ρ near 0 or no monotonicity, and no ΔΔG-prediction advantage over conservation-matched controls, means the representation tracks category not physics, so H3 fails even if H2's binary selectivity held.

Experiment 4 (H1/H2 — Coevolution and PSSM baselines rule out statistics-only explanation): Tests that any observed mechanism-selectivity (H1 features, H2 causal drops) is not explained by coevolutionary statistics alone. Data: for the 300-protein set, compute categorical-Jacobian coevolution couplings from ESM-2 and PSSM/MSA statistics (MSAs from ColabFold's UniRef30 search; existing, no new data). Model: frozen ESM-2; baselines are statistical readouts, not trained networks. Systems compared: mechanism-selectivity index S (Experiment 2) and dose-response ρ (Experiment 3) computed from model features vs from coevolution-coupling features vs PSSM features. Decisive metric first: gap ΔS = S(model feature) − S(coevolution feature). Convincing result: ΔS significantly > 0 — the model's causal selectivity exceeds what couplings/PSSM reproduce. Undecidable band: ΔS in [−0.1, 0.2] — model and coevolution indistinguishable, meaning the apparent mechanism signal is attributable to statistics; band fixed before data and read as failing to isolate a model-specific mechanism. Negative result: coevolution matches or exceeds the model's selectivity, so the earlier positive H1/H2 signals do not demonstrate a representation beyond evolutionary statistics.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 — Layer and scale trajectory of mechanism-selectivity): Tests where the mechanism representation lives and whether scaling makes ESM-2 more mechanistic or more correlational, sharpening rather than enlarging H1/H2. Data: reuse Experiment 1–2 sites; no new data. Model: frozen ESM-2 150M and 650M as main study, with 3B as a compute-permitting extension (SAE on 3B activations is the expensive step; probes on 3B are cheap and always run); every layer's probe AUROC and Experiment-2 selectivity S recorded; 3 seeds. Systems compared: per-layer and per-scale S and AUROC. Decisive metric first: layer of peak S and the sign of the 150M→650M(→3B) trend in peak S. Convincing result: a consistent, reproducible layer band where S peaks, with a monotone scale trend interpretable as more-mechanistic (S rising) or more-correlational (S falling). Undecidable band: |scale slope of peak S| within its 3-seed standard error — reported as "no scale effect", not evidence either way. Negative result: no reproducible peak layer (S within noise across depth) means the earlier selectivity is not stably localized and weakens confidence in H1/H2 rather than adding scope.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Confound: buried-charged mutations also disrupt evolutionary statistics, so mechanism-preserving controls must be carefully matched on conservation change; if matching is imperfect, causal attribution weakens. We mitigate with explicit conservation-matched control mutations.
Features may be distributed/superposed such that no single feature cleanly maps to one mechanism; we address this using both SAE features and probe directions and reporting aggregate directions.
Molecular-mechanics ddG estimates (FoldX) are approximate and may be noisy, limiting the strength of the physics-agreement comparison.

Results may reveal that models are largely correlational; while scientifically valuable, this could be seen as a negative result — we frame it as a definitive answer either way with implications for variant-effect trust.
Access to ESM-2 3B and structure datasets is feasible for an academic lab, but running SAEs on 3B activations is compute-heavy; we scope the main study to 150M/650M with 3B as an extension.

Objects of inference are kept separate: raw ESM-2 activations, SAE features, and linear-probe directions are reported independently rather than merged. When no single feature localizes a mechanism (superposition), we test aggregate subspace directions and pre-register that a mechanism whose best readout lands in the [0.70,0.80] AUROC band is reported as 'inconclusive', reserving 'no causal evidence' for selectivity indices statistically indistinguishable from 1.

Name: cyp450_bypass_ddi_probe
Title: Same Enzyme, Same Danger? Testing Whether Drug Foundation Models Represent the Shared-CYP450 Metabolic Mechanism of Drug-Drug Interactions, Not Just Structural or Co-Mention Similarity
Short Hypothesis: A large and clinically dominant class of drug-drug interactions (DDIs) has an exactly-known pharmacokinetic mechanism: one drug inhibits/induces a specific cytochrome-P450 (CYP450) enzyme that metabolizes a second drug (the substrate), so the pair interacts because they share a metabolic pathway - not because they look alike or are co-mentioned. We hypothesize that if drug/medical foundation models represent this mechanism rather than surface correlation, then (a) PK-interacting pairs will be organized in the model's internal representation by their SHARED CYP isoform even when structurally dissimilar, (b) a metabolic-bypass counterfactual - replacing the substrate with a therapeutically-equivalent drug metabolized by a DIFFERENT enzyme - will abolish the model's internal interaction signal, whereas a control swap that changes structure but keeps the same enzyme will preserve it, and (c) steering along a recovered 'shared-enzyme' direction causally shifts interaction predictions. The enzyme-swap bypass is an exact, mechanism-defining counterfactual that correlation-based DDI benchmarks cannot provide.
Related Work: Two lines bracket the gap. (1) Interpretable DDI predictors - KnowDDI (2023), MolecBioNet (2025), TRACE (2026), LaGAT (2022), MEN/CYP450 (2025), DeepMetab (2025) - build mechanism in by construction (knowledge-graph subgraphs, attention over substructures, curated CYP rules) and validate via edge AUROC or attention heatmaps; none tests what a general drug/medical FM already encodes. (2) Medical-LLM interpretability - 'Medical Interpretability and Knowledge Maps' (2025) reports the striking descriptive finding that in Llama3.3-70B 'drugs cluster better by medical specialty than by mechanism of action'; 'Elucidating Mechanisms of Demographic Bias' (2025) and medical SAE work (2025-2026) recover and intervene on medical concepts. These are descriptive or bias-focused; none tests whether the representation encodes the PK interaction MECHANISM (shared-enzyme competition) versus structural/co-mention correlation, nor uses a causal metabolic-bypass counterfactual. Because structurally similar drugs, co-prescribed drugs, and shared-enzyme drugs are all correlated in clinical text, correlation-based DDI benchmarks cannot separate mechanism from resemblance; our shared-enzyme grouping test, enzyme-swap bypass counterfactual, and causal steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, and they transfer a correlation-vs-mechanism probe into a safety-critical clinical setting. We frame the contribution as a safety-evaluation benchmark for general-purpose drug/medical foundation models on CYP-mediated DDIs -- an enzyme-swap bypass counterfactual plus probe and steering -- not a new DDI predictor, and explicitly distinct from models that bake in CYP rules by construction (KnowDDI, MEN/CYP450, DeepMetab), which cannot reveal what an off-the-shelf FM already encodes. The novel artifact is the combination: the curated bypass / same-enzyme counterfactual dataset, the shared-enzyme probe, and the causal steering test. Named users are clinical pharmacology, DDI screening, medical-model evaluation, and pharmacovigilance.
Abstract: Drug-drug interactions (DDIs) are a leading, preventable cause of adverse drug events, and machine-learning models are increasingly used to flag them. A clinically dominant class of DDIs has an exactly-known pharmacokinetic mechanism: one drug inhibits or induces a specific cytochrome-P450 (CYP450) enzyme that metabolizes another (the substrate), so the pair interacts because they share a metabolic pathway - independent of how structurally similar they are or how often they co-occur in text. This makes DDIs an ideal, high-stakes testbed for whether drug and medical foundation models learn mechanism or surface correlation. Using public representations from a medical LLM (e.g., MedGemma/Llama medical variants), a chemistry drug FM (e.g., ChemBERTa/SMI-TED on drug SMILES), and a molecule-text model, we ask three mechanism-defining questions. First, a shared-enzyme organization probe: are PK-interacting drug pairs grouped in the internal representation by their shared CYP isoform even when structurally dissimilar, beyond what structural or co-mention similarity predicts? Second, and most decisively, a metabolic-bypass counterfactual: replacing a substrate with a therapeutically-equivalent drug metabolized by a DIFFERENT enzyme should abolish the model's internal interaction signal, whereas a structure-changing control swap that keeps the SAME enzyme should preserve it. Third, causal steering: perturbing a recovered shared-enzyme direction should shift interaction predictions in the enzyme-consistent direction. Metrics quantify a shared-enzyme-beyond-structure index, a bypass-vs-same-enzyme causal asymmetry, and a mechanism-based failure predictor. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed models flag DDIs for the right pharmacological reason - critical before clinical use. CYP450-mediated pharmacokinetic interactions account for a large share of clinically serious DDIs, so the stakes are concrete: if models flag DDIs by structural or co-mention resemblance and fail the bypass counterfactual (the null), FM-based DDI screening should not be trusted for novel or structurally-atypical pairs and must be gated by explicit metabolic-pathway checks; if the shared-enzyme mechanism is encoded and steerable, such screening can be trusted for mechanism-consistent cases.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — shared-CYP enzyme organizes interactions beyond structure): Tests assertion (a): pharmacokinetically-interacting drug pairs are organized in the representation by their SHARED cytochrome-P450 isoform even when structurally dissimilar. Data (existing, curated): PK-DDI pairs from DrugBank, the Flockhart CYP450 tables, and the University of Washington Drug Interaction Database, each labeled by responsible isoform (CYP3A4, CYP2D6, CYP2C9, CYP1A2, ...); pharmacodynamic (target-level, no shared enzyme) DDIs collected as a distinct class. These sources yield on the order of 10^3 well-annotated PK pairs; we use up to 1,000 PK pairs and 500 PD pairs, reporting the structurally-dissimilar shared-enzyme subset (ECFP4 Tanimoto < 0.4) separately as the most diagnostic. Models (frozen, inference only): a medical LLM (MedGemma, 4B), ChemBERTa-2 (~46M) on SMILES, and MoleculeSTM (molecule-text); per-drug and per-pair representations. Trainable: linear probes only (3 seeds). Systems compared: model representation vs an ECFP/Tanimoto structural-similarity baseline and a text co-mention-frequency baseline. Decisive metric first: Shared-Enzyme-Beyond-Structure Index = accuracy of decoding 'shared responsible enzyme' from the representation minus what structural + co-mention similarity achieve, after regressing both out. Indecision band up front: an index in [0.03, 0.10] (accuracy points) cannot decide and is reported as ambiguous metabolic-structure encoding; index >= 0.10 with CI lower bound > 0.03, especially on the structurally-dissimilar subset, is convincing enzyme-mechanism encoding; index <= 0.03 means grouping is driven by resemblance, supporting the surface-correlation hypothesis.

Experiment 2 (H2 — metabolic-bypass counterfactual, decisive): Tests assertion (b): replacing the substrate with a therapeutically-equivalent drug metabolized by a DIFFERENT enzyme should abolish the internal interaction signal, whereas a same-enzyme structural swap should preserve it; symmetric on the inhibitor side; and PK-only (a PD interaction should not be abolished by an enzyme bypass). Data (constructed from existing): for each PK-DDI (inhibitor I + substrate S metabolized by enzyme E) restricted to drugs with a single dominant CYP isoform, build (a) a bypass swap S->S_bypass (equivalent indication, different enzyme E') and (b) a same-enzyme control swap S->S_same (structurally different, still enzyme E), matched on structural-change magnitude; repeat on the inhibitor side; include PD pairs as a double-dissociation control. We target ~200 clean single-isoform PK pairs. Model: same three frozen models; interaction signal is a probed interaction score plus, for MedGemma, the interaction likelihood under several prompt templates (representation probe is primary). Systems compared: bypass swap vs same-enzyme swap; PK vs PD. Decisive metric first: Bypass-vs-Same-Enzyme Causal Asymmetry = |signal drop under bypass swap| / |signal change under same-enzyme control|, CI over pairs. Indecision band up front: an asymmetry whose CI lies in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide and is reported as weak mechanism sensitivity; CI lower bound > 2.0, with the PD control showing NO abolition, is convincing shared-enzyme-mechanism encoding; CI upper bound < 1.3 (both swaps change the signal alike) is the surface-feature signature. This is the decisive, safety-relevant test; a null is the headline negative result.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal shared-enzyme steering): Tests assertion (c): steering a drug's representation along a recovered 'CYP-E substrate/inhibitor' direction causally shifts its predicted interaction with a CYP-E inhibitor in the enzyme-consistent direction. Data: single-isoform drugs from Experiment 2. Model: frozen; the enzyme direction is the Experiment 1 probe direction (no backbone training). Procedure: add matched-norm perturbations moving a drug toward/away from 'CYP-E substrate' and read the pairwise interaction prediction; controls are matched-norm random directions and a structural-feature direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |interaction-prediction shift under enzyme direction| / |shift under random direction|, CI over drugs. Indecision band up front: selectivity CI in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide (no clean causal handle); CI lower bound > 2.0 with an enzyme-consistent shift is convincing causal use of the metabolic mechanism; CI upper bound < 1.3 means no separable causal enzyme direction. A negative result, with H1-H2 nulls, supports the surface-correlation conclusion and warns against FM-based DDI screening for structurally-atypical pairs.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Shared-enzyme drugs, co-prescribed drugs, and structurally similar drugs are correlated in clinical text, making the shared-enzyme-beyond-structure separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with structural/co-mention residualization, the enzyme-swap bypass counterfactual (which holds the interacting partner fixed), and matched structural-change controls.

Constructing 'therapeutically-equivalent but different-enzyme' bypass swaps requires curated pharmacology knowledge and clean CYP annotations; some drugs are metabolized by multiple enzymes, blurring the bypass. We restrict counterfactuals to drugs with a single dominant responsible CYP isoform and report sensitivity to isoform-assignment confidence.

For prompted medical LLMs, the 'internal interaction signal' may depend on prompt phrasing; we use multiple prompt templates and both probed representations and generated interaction judgments, treating the representational probe as primary evidence.

Chemistry FMs that pool to a single molecule embedding limit fine-grained substructure analysis; we prioritize models exposing usable per-molecule representations and report pooling caveats, and treat cross-model agreement as supporting rather than definitive.

Steering directions recovered by probes may not be causally used; we address this with steering plus random/structural-direction controls, though distributed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

A negative result (models flag DDIs by structural/co-mention resemblance and fail the bypass counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly safety-relevant - it would warn against trusting FM-based DDI screening for novel or structurally-atypical drug pairs - though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether drug FMs represent the shared-CYP450 mechanism of pharmacokinetic interactions.

Null baselines and selection reporting: we add randomized-enzyme-label probes, random swaps, and non-CYP (pharmacodynamic) DDI controls as nulls the mechanism signal must beat, pre-register the bypass / control matching criteria (indication, class, route, dosage form, structural distance, text frequency), and report coverage and attrition after restricting to single-dominant-CYP pairs to expose selection bias.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public/curated pharmacology databases, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: implicit_electron_flow_probe
Title: Recipes or Mechanisms? Probing Whether Reactant-to-Product Transformers Internally Represent Arrow-Pushing Electron Flow They Were Never Taught
Short Hypothesis: Standard product-prediction transformers (Molecular Transformer / Chemformer trained on USPTO reactant->product SMILES) are widely assumed to learn reactions as 'recipes' rather than mechanisms, which is precisely why an entire line of purpose-built electron-flow models was created. We hypothesize the opposite is partially true at the representational level: even without any mechanistic supervision, these models internally encode the arrow-pushing electron-redistribution structure of a reaction - which atoms are electron donors/acceptors, which bonds form/break, and the direction of electron flow - and that this latent mechanistic structure is causally load-bearing for prediction and predicts where the model generalizes versus hallucinates. If instead they are pure recipe learners, mechanism-defined features (electron source/sink, bond-electron changes) will be no more decodable than shuffled controls, and mechanism-aligned interventions will not selectively affect predictions. We define electron-flow structure operationally as per-atom donor/acceptor role, per-bond formation/breaking, and net electron change from the bond-electron matrix - distinct from generic reaction-center or functional-group detection, which we control for explicitly.
Related Work: Two lines of work bracket this gap. (1) Purpose-built mechanistic models - ELECTRO (2018), non-autoregressive electron redistribution (2021), FlowER (Nature 2025, mass/electron-conserving flow matching), Reactron (2025), DeepMech (2025), PMechRP/ArrowFinder (2025) - are motivated by the explicit premise that standard product-prediction models 'treat reactions as recipes with limited mechanistic insight' and 'hallucinate' because they ignore electron flow. They BUILD mechanism in by construction; they do not ask whether standard models already encode it. (2) Interpretability of chemistry models - 'BERT Learns Chemistry' (attention to reactive functional groups), 'Circuits, Features, and Heuristics in Molecular Transformers' (2025, SAEs/valence circuits on a generative transformer), and the SchNet reaction-analogy paper (2025, constant reaction vectors) - shows chemistry models encode substructures and even reaction-difference directions. But none tests whether a REACTION product-prediction transformer internally represents the ELECTRON-FLOW / bond-electron-matrix mechanism, uses it causally, or whether that structure governs OOD/hallucination behavior. Our contribution is a mechanism-defining, causally-tested probe that uses external mechanistic datasets (mech-USPTO-31k, PMechDB, FlowER's mechanism sequences) - which the product model never saw - as ground truth to arbitrate the 'recipe vs mechanism' debate at the representational level. The contribution is threefold and kept separate: the directional donor-vs-acceptor probe, the causal steering evidence, and the use of external mechanistic labels as held-out ground truth.
Abstract: The dominant machine-learning approach to reaction outcome prediction maps reactant SMILES directly to product SMILES, and a whole research program of electron-flow models has been built on the premise that such models are mere 'recipe' learners that ignore mechanism and therefore hallucinate mass-imbalanced products. Yet whether these product-prediction transformers implicitly encode reaction mechanism internally has never been tested. We ask a simple, mechanism-defining question: does a reactant-to-product transformer, trained without any mechanistic supervision, internally represent the arrow-pushing electron-flow structure of a reaction - the electron sources and sinks, the bonds that form and break, and the direction of electron redistribution? We use pretrained Molecular Transformer and Chemformer as the models under study and treat external mechanism datasets (mech-USPTO-31k, PMechDB, and FlowER's elementary-step sequences) - which these models never saw - as held-out ground truth. First, we train linear probes and sparse autoencoders on internal activations to decode per-atom electron donor/acceptor role, per-bond formation/breaking, and net electron change (from the bond-electron matrix), comparing against strict atom-mapping and reactivity-shuffled controls. Second, we run causal interventions: steering activations along the recovered electron-source or bond-breaking directions should shift predicted products along the mechanistically-correct path, while matched random directions should not. Third, we test whether the strength/consistency of the internal electron-flow representation predicts, per reaction, when the model produces mass-balanced correct products versus hallucinations and how it generalizes out-of-distribution. Either outcome decisively resolves the recipe-versus-mechanism debate at the level of learned representations, informing a concrete decision - whether to trust, probe, or replace standard reaction transformers with purpose-built electron-flow models - and, by tying representation strength to hallucination/OOD behavior, explaining a failure mode that matters for retrosynthesis and synthesis planning.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Electron-flow structure decodable from product-model activations): Tests the H1 claim that reactant→product transformers internally encode arrow-pushing structure (per-atom donor/acceptor role, per-bond form/break, reaction-center membership) that was never in their training data. Data: held-out mechanism ground truth from mech-USPTO-31k (~31k reactions), PMechDB, and FlowER elementary-step bond-electron (BE) matrices; we use 8,000 high-confidence, mass-balanced, atom-mapped reactions — 8,000 gives thousands of labeled atoms/bonds per class while excluding low-confidence mappings; per-atom electron role and per-bond change derived from atom-mapping + BE matrix. None of this annotation was in the product models' training data. Model: pretrained Molecular Transformer and Chemformer (public weights), frozen; trainable = linear probes and SAEs (dictionary 8,192, L1 1e-3) on encoder residual-stream (and decoder cross-attention) activations, per layer; 5 folds, 3 seeds. Systems compared: model-activation probe vs baselines — raw one-hot atom/bond features, Morgan fingerprints, a functional-group-only baseline, a matched reaction-center baseline (given reaction-center membership, is the donor/acceptor direction still decodable?), a probe-capacity control (matched-capacity probe fit on shuffled labels), and a reactivity-shuffled control (electron roles permuted across same-type atoms). Decisive metric first: probe accuracy/F1 for donor/acceptor role, bond form/break, and reaction-center membership, minus the shuffled-control and fingerprint baselines. Convincing result: F1 ≥ 0.75 for all three targets, exceeding fingerprint and shuffled baselines by a clear margin. Undecidable band: model-minus-baseline F1 gap in [0.0, 0.05] — decodability attributable to substructure identity, not mechanism, reported as unsupported for that target; band fixed before data. Negative result: probes no better than shuffled/fingerprint controls means no decodable electron-flow structure, H1 fails and H2/H3 are moot.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Directional donor-vs-acceptor within the reaction center): Tests the stricter H1 sub-claim that the model encodes electron-flow direction, not merely reactive-site location. Data: the reaction-center atoms of the 8,000 reactions, labeled donor vs acceptor. Model: frozen Molecular Transformer / Chemformer, fixed Experiment-1 activations; probe restricted to atoms already known to be in the reaction center; 3 seeds. Systems compared: donor-vs-acceptor classifier vs chance (both are reactive, so location cannot help) and vs the shuffled-role control. Decisive metric first: donor-vs-acceptor classification accuracy conditioned on reaction-center membership. Convincing result: accuracy ≥ 0.75, well above the 0.5 chance floor and above the shuffled control. Undecidable band: accuracy in [0.55, 0.65] — weak directional signal, reported as inconclusive; band fixed before data. Negative result: accuracy ≈ 0.5 means the model flags where reaction happens but not the electron-flow direction, so H1's directional core fails even if reaction-center localization succeeded.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Causal steering along electron-flow directions): Tests the H2 claim that electron-flow structure is causally load-bearing — steering an atom toward 'donor' shifts predicted products toward mechanisms where it donates electrons. Data: 1,000 reactions from the Experiment-1 test split (1,000 keeps the α-sweep × seed × decode grid affordable). Model: frozen models with fixed Experiment-1 donor/acceptor and bond-breaking directions; add ±α·(unit direction) to the atom's activations at the best-F1 layer, α over {0.5,1,2}× activation std; decode products; 3 seeds. Systems compared: true-direction steering vs matched-norm random-direction control, a non-mechanistic latent-direction control (an unrelated decoded direction), and an input-level counterfactual baseline (editing the reactant SMILES to change the donor/acceptor atom) as an upper reference for the expected product change. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity index M = |effect_true direction| / |effect_random direction|, plus the fraction of interventions producing the mechanistically-predicted product change and SMILES validity rate. Convincing result: M ≥ 3 with predicted-change fraction well above the random control and validity ≥ 0.8. Undecidable band: M in [1.2, 2.0] or validity < 0.5 (off-manifold) — reported as inconclusive; band fixed before data. Negative result: M ≈ 1 means directions are decodable but not causal, H2 fails.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Representation strength predicts hallucination and OOD accuracy): Tests the H3 claim that electron-flow representation strength predicts where the model generalizes vs hallucinates, and checks internal electron/mass conservation. Data: the 8,000 reactions plus held-out OOD reaction classes (reaction types withheld from USPTO training splits); model-predicted products labeled correct/mass-balanced vs hallucinated. Model: frozen models; per-reaction 'electron-flow strength' = probe confidence / SAE feature coherence over the reaction center; also probe net-electron conservation (electrons removed at breaking bonds vs added at forming bonds). Systems compared: electron-flow strength vs baselines — output token log-probability and deep-ensemble variance. Decisive metric first: AUROC for flagging hallucinated (mass-imbalanced/incorrect) products from electron-flow strength, and Spearman ρ with per-reaction accuracy on OOD classes. Convincing result: AUROC ≥ 0.75 and above both baselines by ≥ 0.05, with probed conservation-consistency higher on correct than hallucinated reactions. Undecidable band: AUROC within 0.03 of the best baseline — no representation-specific predictive value, reported as not distinguishable from confidence heuristics; band fixed before data. Negative result: electron-flow strength at chance or below baselines means the structure does not predict generalization/hallucination, H3 fails.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 — Layer/emergence, cross-model convergence, and recipe-to-mechanism brackets): Locates the structure and places the product models on the recipe-to-mechanism spectrum without enlarging the claim. Data: the 8,000-reaction set. Model: frozen Molecular Transformer and Chemformer, per-layer and encoder-vs-decoder analysis; brackets = a mechanism-supervised model's representations (FlowER, upper) and a model trained on shuffled reactant–product pairs (lower), each probed identically; CKA between the two product models' recovered electron-flow subspaces; 3 seeds. Systems compared: per-layer probe F1 and steering M across depth/components; product-model decodability vs FlowER upper and shuffled lower brackets. Decisive metric first: layer/component of peak electron-flow decodability, mean pairwise CKA, and where product-model F1 falls between the shuffled lower and FlowER upper brackets. Convincing result: a reproducible peak layer, CKA ≥ 0.6 (convergent), and product-model F1 clearly above the shuffled lower bracket. Undecidable band: CKA in [0.3, 0.45] or product-model F1 within noise of the shuffled bracket — reported as weakly convergent / no advantage over recipe-learning; band fixed before data. Negative result: product-model decodability at the shuffled-pair bracket means they are genuine recipe learners, bounding H1/H2 and (as noted) justifying the purpose-built mechanistic-model program.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Atom-mapping errors in USPTO-derived mechanism annotations introduce label noise into probes; we restrict to high-confidence atom-mapped and mass-balanced reactions (mech-USPTO-31k, FlowER, PMechDB) and report sensitivity to mapping confidence.

Decodability of electron roles could reflect trivial correlation with atom/functional-group identity rather than genuine mechanistic representation; we control with reactivity-shuffled labels, within-reaction-center donor-vs-acceptor tests, and fingerprint baselines, and rely on causal steering as the primary mechanism evidence.

Steering in a nonlinear seq2seq transformer may push activations off-manifold and produce invalid SMILES; we bound alpha, report validity rates and sensitivity to alpha, and use matched random-direction controls.
Distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions; we use both linear probe directions and SAE features and report aggregate-direction effects.

A negative result (product models are genuinely recipe learners with no decodable, causal electron-flow structure) is scientifically decisive - it would justify the purpose-built mechanistic-model program - though it may be perceived as confirmatory; we frame either outcome as resolving the recipe-vs-mechanism debate at the representational level.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public datasets, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: temporal_directionality_ehr_probe
Title: A Then B, Not B Then A: Testing Whether EHR Foundation Models Represent the Temporal Directionality of Disease Progression, Not Just Symmetric Co-occurrence
Short Hypothesis: Disease progression is a directed, temporally asymmetric mechanism: the trajectory diabetes -> nephropathy -> renal failure is causal and irreversible, whereas its reverse is clinically nonsensical, and this directionality (not mere co-occurrence) is what determines prognosis and treatment. We hypothesize that if EHR foundation models represent the progression mechanism rather than symmetric co-occurrence statistics, then (a) the temporal direction of a diagnosis pair (A-before-B vs B-before-A) is decodable from internal representations beyond what unordered co-occurrence predicts, (b) an exact sequence-reversal counterfactual - reversing only the order of two events while holding their identities, times-between, and all else fixed - flips the internal risk/prognosis signal for directed (progression) pairs but not for order-invariant (comorbidity) pairs, and (c) steering a recovered 'progression-direction' axis causally shifts downstream risk predictions. The reversal counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that predictive accuracy and attention-pathway alignment cannot provide.
Related Work: EHR foundation models built on next-event prediction (NEP EHR FM 2025; Sequential Pattern Transformer 2026) report attention patterns that 'align with known disease pathways,' and trajectory-mining work (All of Us ordered-sequence discovery 2025; directed hypergraphs of multimorbidity 2023; THCM-CAL 2025) shows ordered A->B->C sequences carry risk beyond bag-of-codes. Clinical causal-discovery methods (EHR causal structure learning 2021; LLM edge-directionality in NSCLC 2023) and symptom-causality probes (CausaLM/TReATE for chest pain 2025) estimate causal effects at the output level. Crucially, the systematic single-cell FM evaluation (2026) and 'Medical Interpretability and Knowledge Maps' (2025) show these models' internals often capture co-occurrence rather than causal/mechanistic structure, and that disease-progression representations can be circular/non-monotonic. But no work tests whether an EHR foundation model's INTERNAL representation encodes the TEMPORAL DIRECTIONALITY (A-before-B vs B-before-A asymmetry) that defines progression, whether that directionality is causally load-bearing, or uses an exact sequence-reversal counterfactual to separate directed progression from symmetric comorbidity. Because directed pairs and mere comorbid pairs both show high co-occurrence, predictive benchmarks and attention-pathway alignment cannot arbitrate this. Our directionality-beyond-co-occurrence probe, sequence-reversal counterfactual, and causal progression-direction steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, transferred into a safety-critical clinical setting where getting the arrow backwards inverts prognosis. Stated precisely, the contribution is representational and causal, not a new order-sensitive predictor: a falsifiable test (the exact sequence-reversal counterfactual plus a directed-vs-comorbidity double dissociation and progression-direction steering) of whether an EHR FM's internal representation encodes temporal directionality, reported as evidence for or against encoding rather than definitive clinical causality. Order-pretraining and trajectory-mining work shows ordered sequences carry predictive risk at the output level; none tests internal directionality via reversal. A concrete failure: a model reading symmetric co-occurrence would assign a patient recorded as renal-failure-then-diabetes the same trajectory risk as the true diabetes-then-renal-failure, inverting prognosis and mis-triaging atypically-ordered patients. Who would cite it: model auditors, EHR-FM developers, and clinical risk-prediction researchers.
Abstract: Electronic health record (EHR) foundation models trained by next-event prediction are increasingly used to forecast disease progression and clinical risk, and their attention patterns reportedly align with known disease pathways. But a pathway is not merely a set of co-occurring diagnoses: it is a directed, temporally asymmetric mechanism, where diabetes preceding kidney failure carries a prognosis that its reverse does not. Because predictive accuracy and attention-alignment cannot distinguish encoding this directionality from encoding symmetric co-occurrence, whether these models represent the progression mechanism is untested. We propose the first mechanism-defining test. Using public EHR foundation models trained on MIMIC-III/IV and, where available, larger event-sequence models, we ask three questions. First, a directionality-beyond-co-occurrence probe: is the temporal order of a diagnosis pair (A-before-B vs B-before-A) decodable from internal representations beyond what unordered co-occurrence predicts? Second, and most decisively, a sequence-reversal counterfactual: for matched patient trajectories we reverse only the order of two events - holding their identities, inter-event times, and surrounding context fixed - and test whether the internal risk/prognosis signal flips for directed progression pairs (e.g., nephropathy->renal-failure) but stays stable for order-invariant comorbidity pairs (e.g., hypertension and hyperlipidemia); a co-occurrence-statistics model responds identically to both. Third, causal steering along a recovered progression-direction axis should shift downstream risk. Metrics quantify a directionality-beyond-co-occurrence index, a reversal-vs-comorbidity causal asymmetry, and a mechanism-based failure predictor. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed clinical models understand which way the arrow points. If confirmed, temporal-reversal robustness becomes a model-selection and auditing criterion for clinical risk models; if refuted, it flags that deployed models may confuse cause with consequence, motivating order-aware objectives and reversal-based evaluation rather than reliance on predictive AUC alone.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — temporal direction decodable beyond unordered co-occurrence): Tests clause (a): the temporal direction of a diagnosis pair (A-before-B vs B-before-A) is decodable from internal representations beyond what unordered co-occurrence predicts. Data: timestamped diagnosis/procedure/medication sequences from MIMIC-III (~40k patients) and MIMIC-IV (~300k); curate ~50 DIRECTED progression pairs with clinically established, largely irreversible order (e.g., diabetic nephropathy -> end-stage renal failure; hypertension -> heart failure; adenoma -> colorectal cancer) and ~50 ORDER-INVARIANT comorbidity pairs (e.g., hypertension & hyperlipidemia), then extract patient trajectories containing each pair — targeting ≥1,000 trajectories per pair class (split by patient), restricting directed pairs to large time gaps across separate admissions to reduce coding-order artifacts. Model: an event-sequence next-event-prediction transformer trained on MIMIC (~tens of M parameters, per-event representations) and a bag-of-codes baseline model, frozen; a logistic order-probe on the best layer, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: order-decoding from the representation vs an unordered co-occurrence/prevalence baseline, representation residualized against co-occurrence, reported separately for directed vs comorbidity pairs. Decisive metric (first): Directionality-Beyond-Co-occurrence Index = order-classification accuracy(representation) − accuracy(co-occurrence features). Convincing: Index ≥ 0.10 (95% CI lower bound above 0.03) for directed pairs and ≤ 0.03 for comorbidity pairs (double dissociation). Indecision band: Index in [−0.02, 0.03] for directed pairs — within probe noise; clause (a) fails here. Negative result: Index ≤ −0.02 or in band for directed pairs — the model encodes symmetric co-occurrence, not order.

Experiment 2 (H2 — sequence-reversal counterfactual with prognosis-sign consistency): Tests clause (b): reversing only the order of two events (holding identities, inter-event time, and all else fixed) flips the internal risk/prognosis signal for directed pairs but not for comorbidity pairs. Data: matched patient trajectories from Experiment 1 (≥1,000 per pair class); for each, build (true order A-before-B) and (reversed order B-before-A) by swapping only the two events' positions/timestamps. Model/probe as Experiment 1, seeds 0–4; read-out is a probed risk score and the model's outcome head (e.g., predicted mortality or downstream complication). Systems compared: |signal change under reversal| for directed vs for comorbidity pairs; plus the signed comparison forward-order risk vs reversed-order risk for directed pairs. Decisive metrics (first): Reversal-vs-Comorbidity Causal Asymmetry = median(|Δsignal directed|) / median(|Δsignal comorbidity|); and Prognosis-Sign Consistency = fraction of directed pairs with forward-order risk exceeding reversed-order risk. Convincing: asymmetry ≥ 3 and prognosis-sign consistency ≥ 0.8, while comorbidity pairs show near-zero directed difference. Indecision band: asymmetry in [0.7, 2.0] or prognosis-sign consistency in [0.5, 0.65] — order barely matters; clause (b) fails or is inconclusive here. Negative result: asymmetry ≈ 1 and consistency ≈ 0.5 — forward and reversed progressions read alike, a co-occurrence-statistics representation.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal progression-direction steering): Tests clause (c): steering a recovered 'progression-direction' axis causally shifts downstream risk predictions. Data: the directed-pair trajectories from Experiment 2; the axis is recovered as a supervised order-probe direction and a delta-representation between forward-order and reversed-order versions. Model/probe as above; add matched-norm perturbations along the axis at the best layer and read the risk head, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: progression-direction axis vs matched-norm random directions vs a co-occurrence-magnitude direction. Decisive metric (first): Steering Selectivity = |Δrisk from progression-direction steering| / |Δrisk from random-direction steering|. Convincing: selectivity ≥ 3 with the progression-consistent sign and the co-occurrence direction not reproducing it. Indecision band: selectivity in [0.7, 2.0] — no better than random; clause (c) fails here. Negative result: selectivity ≈ 1 — no dedicated causal progression-direction axis.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Recorded event order in EHRs is a noisy proxy for true clinical onset order (billing/coding order, batched diagnoses, same-admission codes with identical timestamps); we mitigate by restricting directed pairs to those with large, clinically meaningful time gaps across separate admissions, using validated ordered-trajectory resources, and reporting sensitivity to timestamp-quality thresholds.

Directed progression pairs and order-invariant comorbidity pairs both have high co-occurrence, making the directionality-beyond-co-occurrence separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with co-occurrence residualization, the sequence-reversal counterfactual (which holds identities and timing fixed and varies only order), and the directed-vs-comorbidity double dissociation.

The reversal counterfactual creates clinically implausible trajectories that may fall off the model's training distribution, confounding the reversal response with generic out-of-distribution behavior; we mitigate by comparing directed-pair reversals against comorbidity-pair reversals of matched implausibility/edit-magnitude (both are edited, so any generic OOD effect is shared) and reporting edit-magnitude sensitivity.

Some EHR foundation models tokenize events without fine-grained timestamps or use position-invariant pooling, limiting access to order; we document each model's temporal encoding, prioritize models that ingest ordered/timestamped sequences, and treat pooling-invariant models as an informative lower bracket that by construction cannot represent direction.

Ground-truth causal direction for some pairs is debated or bidirectional; we restrict decisive tests to well-established, largely irreversible progressions and report sensitivity to pair-confidence thresholds.

Linear probes recovering a progression-direction axis do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/co-occurrence-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we use both probe directions and delta-representations.

A negative result (models encode symmetric co-occurrence and respond identically to forward vs reversed progression, failing the reversal counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly safety-relevant - it would warn that deployed clinical risk models may not distinguish cause from consequence, risking inverted prognoses and inappropriate interventions for atypically-ordered patients; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether EHR foundation models represent the temporal directionality of disease progression.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public EHR datasets (MIMIC-III/IV) with validated trajectory resources, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: reproduction_number_threshold_probe
Title: Above or Below One? Testing Whether Epidemic Time-Series Foundation Models Represent the Reproduction-Number Threshold Mechanism, Not Just Curve Momentum
Short Hypothesis: The defining mechanism of epidemic dynamics is the effective reproduction number R_t and its exact threshold at R_t=1: R_t>1 implies growth, R_t<1 implies decline, and the same recent case curve can be heading up or down depending only on R_t (e.g., a peak plateau vs. an inflection). Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) now used for epidemic forecasting and policy counterfactuals are trained to extrapolate curve shape, which never requires learning this threshold. We hypothesize that if a TSFM represents the epidemic mechanism rather than curve momentum, then (a) R_t and its side relative to 1 are decodable from internal representations beyond what the recent curve shape/slope predicts, (b) an R-holding counterfactual (matched recent curve, opposite R_t side) will be internally distinguished and forecast in opposite directions, and (c) steering a recovered 'R-threshold' direction causally flips growth-vs-decline forecasts. The matched-curve/opposite-R counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that curve-fitting cannot pass.
Related Work: Recent work shows TSFMs (Chronos, TimesFM, TimeGPT, TabPFN-TS, Lag-Llama) forecast epidemics well and even produce policy counterfactuals ('Foundation time series models for forecasting and policy evaluation', 2025), and epidemiology-aware pretrained models exist (CAPE, 2025, with 'compartmental prototypes'). Physics-informed and hybrid mechanistic-neural models (EINNs 2023; PINN-SIR 2025; hybrid neural-ODE 2026) BUILD R/SIR structure in by construction. TSFM interpretability shows encoded, steerable concepts: time2time (2025) causally implants 'crash/regime' semantics and finds severity encoded as a continuous latent; 'Exploring Representations...' (2024) and 'On the Internal Semantics of TSFMs' (2025) recover linear trend/periodicity/level-shift concepts. Crucially, none tests whether a TSFM internally represents the reproduction-number threshold mechanism (R_t vs. 1) that governs whether an epidemic grows or declines, nor uses a matched-curve/opposite-R counterfactual to separate this mechanism from mere growth momentum. Because R_t and recent curve slope are correlated in ordinary data, correlation-based forecasting benchmarks cannot arbitrate this; our threshold probe, R-holding counterfactual, and causal R-steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, transferred into a safety-critical public-health setting. The novelty is a mechanistic-interpretability benchmark for epidemic TSFMs, not a new forecasting method: the single falsifiable primary claim is that internal representations contain information about sign(R_t - 1) beyond every short-window shape statistic used by the baseline (slope, curvature, short AR fit). It is distinct from prior latent-concept probes (trend/periodicity/regime) and from forecasting-accuracy benchmarks, neither of which isolates the threshold. We soften 'represents the mechanism' to 'encodes separable information about the R_t=1 threshold' unless the steering test is convincingly direction-specific.
Abstract: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) are increasingly used to forecast infectious-disease epidemics and even to evaluate public-health policies through counterfactual scenarios. Yet epidemic dynamics are defined by an exact, threshold-based mechanism: the effective reproduction number R_t, whose value relative to 1 determines whether cases grow or decline. Because TSFMs are trained to extrapolate observed curve shape, they can succeed by learning growth momentum without ever internalizing the R_t=1 threshold. This distinction is decision-critical: the most consequential forecasts are precisely at turning points, where recent curve shape is ambiguous and only R_t settles the direction. We propose the first mechanism-defining test of whether epidemic-forecasting TSFMs represent the reproduction-number mechanism. Using synthetic SIR/SEIR trajectories (where R_t is exactly known and controllable) and real surveillance data with estimated R_t, we probe pretrained TSFMs (Chronos, TimesFM, Lag-Llama, and the epidemiology-aware CAPE). First, a threshold-beyond-momentum probe: can R_t and its side relative to 1 be decoded from internal representations beyond what recent slope/curvature predicts? Second, and most decisively, an R-holding counterfactual: we construct trajectory pairs with near-identical recent curves but opposite R_t sides (one approaching a peak from below, one just past it), so momentum is matched but mechanism is opposite; a mechanistic representation must separate them and forecast opposite directions. Third, causal steering along a recovered R-threshold direction should flip growth-vs-decline forecasts. Metrics quantify a threshold-beyond-momentum index, a matched-curve turning-point asymmetry, and a steering flip rate. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed epidemic TSFMs forecast for the right mechanistic reason. Why it matters now: the most consequential epidemic forecasts and TSFM-based policy counterfactuals are made at turning points, where recent curve shape is ambiguous and only R_t settles the direction, so a momentum-following model will confidently mis-call whether cases are about to grow or decline. The concrete downstream action if the test fails is to require explicit mechanistic (R_t-aware) validation before any TSFM is used for epidemic policy counterfactuals. Intended users are TSFM developers, public-health ML researchers, and benchmark authors; we pre-register success/failure criteria for the threshold probe, counterfactual, and steering tests.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — R_t and its threshold side decodable beyond curve momentum): Tests assertion (a): the reproduction number R_t and its side relative to 1 are decodable from internal representations beyond what recent curve shape/slope predicts. Data (constructed + existing): synthetic SIR/SEIR/SAIRD trajectories with exactly-known time-varying R_t (varying transmission and recovery rates) spanning growth (R_t>1), decline (R_t<1), and turning-point regimes -- we generate >= 20,000 windows; plus real surveillance series (influenza-like illness, RSV, COVID-19, dengue) with published EpiEstim R_t estimates as a transfer/robustness check. Split by trajectory (no trajectory crosses splits). Models (frozen, inference only): general time-series foundation models Chronos, TimesFM, and Lag-Llama, and the epidemiology-aware CAPE; per-timestep representations, preprocessing documented, pre-normalization activations probed where feasible. Trainable: ridge linear probes (L2 by CV, 3 seeds). Systems compared: representation probe vs momentum features computed from the input window (recent slope, curvature, short-window AR fit). Decisive metric first: Threshold-Beyond-Momentum Index = R_t-side classification accuracy (and continuous-R_t R^2) from the representation minus what momentum features achieve, after regressing out the momentum-predictable component. Indecision band up front: an index in [0.03, 0.10] (accuracy points) cannot decide and is reported as ambiguous threshold encoding; index >= 0.10 with CI lower bound > 0.03 is convincing R_t encoding beyond momentum; index <= 0.03 means the model carries only curve momentum, supporting the curve-fitting hypothesis.

Experiment 2 (H2 — R-holding counterfactual and threshold locality, decisive): Tests assertion (b): matched recent curves with opposite R_t sides are internally distinguished and forecast in opposite directions, and the internal change localizes at R_t=1. Data (constructed): matched trajectory pairs whose recent observed windows are made near-indistinguishable by the synthetic generator (matched level, slope, curvature) but that sit on opposite R_t sides -- e.g., approaching a peak from below (R_t just above 1) vs just past the peak (R_t just below 1); residual window-matching error quantified and swept. Plus a sweep of R_t across a range to test where the internal growth-vs-decline signal changes. Model: same frozen TSFMs. Systems compared: opposite-R pairs vs same-R control pairs matched on recent shape; and the transition location vs the true threshold at 1. Decisive metric first: Matched-Curve Separation Ratio = representational distance(opposite-R pair) / representational distance(same-R control), and Turning-Point Direction Accuracy = fraction of opposite-R pairs where the model forecasts growth for the R>1 member and decline for the R<1 member. Indecision band up front: a separation ratio whose CI lies in [1.1, 1.5], or direction accuracy CI in [0.5, 0.65], cannot decide and is reported as momentum-following; ratio CI lower bound > 1.5 WITH direction accuracy CI lower bound > 0.65 and the internal transition localized near R_t=1 (not at arbitrary R_t) is convincing threshold encoding; ratio CI upper bound < 1.1 with direction accuracy CI upper bound < 0.5 (near the 0.5 chance line, following shared shape) is the momentum signature. This is the decisive test; a null is the headline safety-relevant negative result at turning points.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal R-threshold steering and policy-counterfactual faithfulness): Tests assertion (c): steering a recovered R-threshold direction causally flips growth-vs-decline forecasts, and the model's response to an R-reducing intervention is mechanism-consistent. Data: synthetic trajectories sitting near the threshold, with known SIR counterfactuals for an R-reducing intervention. Model: frozen; the R-threshold direction is a supervised probe or a delta-representation between matched R>1 and R<1 states, no backbone training. Procedure: add matched-magnitude perturbations along the R direction and read whether the forecast flips growth<->decline (controls: matched-norm random directions and a pure recent-slope direction); separately, apply an R-reducing intervention and compare the model's counterfactual turning behavior against the true post-intervention R_t side. Decisive metric first: Steering Flip Rate = fraction of steers producing the R-consistent forecast flip, and mechanism-selectivity = |effect of R direction| / |effect of random direction|; plus correlation between model counterfactual turning and true post-intervention R_t side. Indecision band up front: selectivity CI in [1.3, 2.0], or flip rate CI spanning 0.5, cannot decide (no clean causal handle); selectivity CI lower bound > 2.0 with flip rate > 0.6 and counterfactual correlation CI lower bound > 0.5 is convincing causal threshold encoding; selectivity CI upper bound < 1.3 means no separable causal R direction and unfaithful policy counterfactuals. A negative result, with H1-H2 nulls, warns against TSFM epidemic policy counterfactuals precisely at turning points.
Risk Factors and Limitations: R_t and recent curve slope are correlated in ordinary trajectories, making the threshold-beyond-momentum separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with momentum-residualization, the R-holding counterfactual (which matches the recent curve exactly in the synthetic generator), and the threshold-locality control that a momentum model cannot reproduce.

Real-data R_t is an estimate (method- and delay-dependent), adding label noise; we use synthetic data with exactly-known R_t for the primary decisive tests and treat real surveillance as a robustness/transfer check, reporting sensitivity to the R_t estimator.

Constructing near-identical recent windows with opposite R_t requires careful synthetic generation (matching level, slope, curvature over the input window); residual differences could leak the side. We quantify and report the residual matching error and show results as a function of match tightness.

TSFMs normalize/tokenize input series (scaling, patching), which may discard absolute-level information relevant to R; we document each model's preprocessing, probe pre-normalization activations where feasible, and prioritize models exposing per-timestep representations.

Linear probes recovering an R direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/slope-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

A negative result (models forecast from curve momentum and fail the matched-curve/opposite-R counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly safety-relevant, warning against trusting TSFM epidemic forecasts and policy counterfactuals precisely at turning points where they matter most; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether epidemic TSFMs represent the reproduction-number threshold.

Oracle and null baselines: the momentum baseline uses oracle recent-slope/curvature features, and we add random-label probes and matched-pair leakage audits (quantifying residual window-matching error) so a positive threshold-beyond-momentum result cannot be an artifact; ablations sweep window length, preprocessing / normalization, and model family.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and standard epidemic simulators / public surveillance data, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: backdoor_confounder_flip_probe
Title: Does the Model Adjust for Confounders? Testing Whether Tabular/Scientific Foundation Models Represent the Backdoor Simpson's-Flip Mechanism, Not Just Observational Association
Short Hypothesis: The mechanism-defining feature that separates causation from correlation is confounder adjustment: the backdoor criterion says the interventional effect P(Y|do(X)) can differ in sign from the observational association P(Y|X) once a common cause (confounder) is adjusted for - the Simpson's-paradox sign flip. We hypothesize that if a tabular/scientific foundation model (e.g., TabPFN, pretrained over structural causal models) internally represents this adjustment mechanism rather than raw observational association, then (a) the adjusted (interventional) effect direction is decodable from internal representations beyond what the observational association predicts, (b) a confounder-presence counterfactual - supplying versus withholding the confounding variable, holding all else fixed - flips the model's internal effect signal in the Simpson's-flip cases but not in confounder-free cases, and (c) steering a recovered 'adjustment' direction causally moves predictions toward the do-calculus answer. The confounder-in-vs-out sign-flip is an exact, mechanism-defining test that predictive accuracy and observational correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: TabPFN, pretrained on synthetic structural-causal-model datasets, is the natural testbed: 'Does TabPFN Understand Causal Structures?' (2025) shows its mid-layer embeddings contain decodable causal-graph information and beat statistical causal-discovery baselines, but it decodes the STATIC adjacency graph - it never tests whether the model represents the ADJUSTMENT mechanism (backdoor/Simpson's-flip) that distinguishes observational from interventional effects, nor uses a confounder-presence counterfactual. 'How Transformers Learn Causal Structure' (2024) and 'Causal Interpretation of Self-Attention' (2023) show transformers encode latent causal graphs in attention, again structural not adjustment-focused. Benchmark studies (CLadder 2023, CausalPitfalls 2025, 'Ice Cream Doesn't Cause Drowning' 2025, contingency-judgment 2025) show LLMs FAIL at confounding and Simpson's paradox at the OUTPUT/prompt level, but none probes internal representations or performs a causal confounder-in/out counterfactual. My own single-cell d-separation probe tested conditional-independence structure but not the sign-flipping backdoor-adjustment mechanism or a confounder-presence intervention. Because observational association and adjusted effect coincide in confounder-free data, correlation-based benchmarks cannot arbitrate this; the adjusted-effect-beyond-observational probe, confounder-in-vs-out sign-flip counterfactual, and causal adjustment-direction steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution.
Abstract: The single most important distinction in causal inference - and the dominant failure mode of data-driven science - is confounder adjustment: an observed association between a variable X and outcome Y can vanish or even reverse sign once a common cause (confounder) is accounted for, the phenomenon known as Simpson's paradox, formalized by the backdoor criterion. Because a model can predict Y well while relying entirely on the confounded observational association, whether foundation models internally represent the adjustment mechanism is untested and safety-critical: confounding by indication, batch, or population dominates errors in drug-response, clinical, and materials data. We propose the first mechanism-defining, representational test. Using TabPFN - a tabular foundation model pretrained over structural causal models - and a general tabular baseline, we generate datasets with known causal graphs where the observational X-Y association and the true interventional (backdoor-adjusted) effect are controllably concordant or sign-discordant (Simpson's-flip). First, an adjusted-effect-beyond-observational probe: is the true interventional effect direction decodable from internal representations beyond what the observational association predicts, along a distinct axis? Second, and most decisively, a confounder-presence counterfactual: we supply versus withhold the confounding variable, holding all else fixed, and test whether the model's internal effect signal flips toward the adjusted answer specifically in Simpson's-flip cases, while confounder-free cases stay stable; an association-only model responds identically. Third, causal steering of a recovered adjustment direction. Metrics quantify an adjustment-beyond-observational index, a confounder-in-vs-out flip asymmetry, and an interventional-fidelity dose-response. Either outcome sharpens whether these models distinguish do(X) from X. The novelty is sharp against the closest TabPFN work, which decodes the static causal graph: we test whether the adjustment mechanism itself is represented AND causally usable, with an explicit minimum criterion for mechanism over conditional-association use, a correct sign flip specific to Simpson's-flip cases, a distinct decoding axis, and a dose-response sign-crossing, none of which a naive conditioner passes. The deliverable is threefold and stated as such: a sign-flip/backdoor benchmark we release, a probe family, and an empirical finding about TabPFN, framed as an evaluation standard for causal competence rather than a single-model case study. Concrete decisions hinge on it, treatment-effect screening, covariate-inclusion policy, and trust calibration for scientific FMs in confounded domains, and both outcomes are actionable: a pass licenses cautious causal-effect use, a fail warns against it.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- the backdoor-adjusted interventional effect direction is decodable beyond observational association): Tests clause (a). Data (constructed, because no public dataset pairs tables with exact do-calculus ground truth across matched confounding regimes): 3,000 synthetic datasets from known structural causal models, 1,000 per regime -- (i) confounder-free (observational X-Y association equals the true interventional effect), (ii) magnitude-confounded (adjustment shrinks but preserves the sign), and (iii) Simpson's-flip (a common cause Z makes the observational X-Y association OPPOSITE in sign to the true backdoor-adjusted P(Y|do(X))). For each we record the causal graph, the observational association, and the exact do-calculus effect. Model: TabPFN (~25M parameters, pretrained over structural causal models, per-layer embeddings accessible) and a general tabular baseline (a supervised MLP/gradient-boosting embedding or tabular transformer), public/standard, frozen; only linear probes trained. Probes: logistic (adjusted-effect direction), L2 via 5-fold CV, 5 seeds with dataset-grouped splits; report mean +/- SD. Systems compared: (i) an observational baseline predicting the interventional effect direction from the observational association alone (wrong in Simpson's-flip cases); (ii) Adjustment-Beyond-Observational Index = adjusted-effect accuracy from the representation minus the observational-baseline accuracy, after residualizing the observational-predictable component, reported separately on the Simpson's-flip subset; (iii) angle between the recovered observational-association and adjusted-effect directions. Decisive metric first: Adjustment-Beyond-Observational Index on the flip subset (accuracy points). Convincing: Index >= 10 points (95% bootstrap CI over held-out datasets excluding 0, >=4/5 seeds) AND axis angle >= 60 degrees (distinct axes). Refute: Index <= 2 points and angle <= 20 degrees. Indeterminate band: 2-10 points or angle 20-60 degrees (stated before the data): unresolved -- some adjustment signal but not a cleanly separate axis; reported as such. A negative result means the model encodes only observational association, contradicting clause (a).

Experiment 2 (H2 -- confounder-in-vs-out counterfactual, with a confounder-free control and semi-realistic transfer): Tests clause (b), the decisive counterfactual. Data: from the synthetic sets (reused) each dataset is presented two ways holding the data-generating process fixed -- confounder-in (Z included as an observed column) and confounder-out (Z withheld, so backdoor adjustment is impossible). As a matched control against generic schema change, in confounder-FREE datasets we instead withhold an equally-informative NON-confounding column (which should not flip the effect). We add a semi-realistic transfer check on tables where the adjusted effect is known/estimable (confounding-by-indication in a drug-outcome table; batch confounding in an omics table). Model: frozen TabPFN and the tabular baseline; effect-direction probe from Experiment 1 reused. Systems compared: internal effect signal confounder-in vs confounder-out, in Simpson's-flip vs confounder-free cases. Decisive metric first: Confounder-In-vs-Out Flip Asymmetry = fraction of Simpson's-flip cases whose internal effect signal moves toward the correct sign-flipped adjusted answer when Z is supplied, contrasted with the near-zero change in confounder-free/control cases. Convincing: flip-toward-correct fraction >= 0.8 in flip cases with the confounder-free control change near 0 (< 0.2), and the semi-realistic tables trending the same way. Refute: flip-toward-correct fraction <= 0.4, or equal movement in the control (a schema-change artifact). Indeterminate band 0.4-0.8 (declared up front): partial support, reported as qualified. A negative result means the model does not adjust when the confounder is present, contradicting clause (b).

Experiment 3 (H2 -- interventional-fidelity dose-response sign-crossing): Strengthens clause (b) by testing that the internal signal tracks the do-calculus effect across the sign change rather than the observational association. Data: synthetic datasets (reused) with confounding strength (Z-to-X and Z-to-Y coupling) varied continuously from zero through the sign-flip threshold, with the true do-calculus effect as ground truth. Model: frozen TabPFN/baseline with the adjusted-effect signal. Systems compared: internal adjusted-effect signal vs true interventional effect across the dose ladder; shuffled-confounder control; the observational association as a foil. Decisive metric first: Spearman correlation between the internal signal and the true interventional effect, plus sign-crossing-location agreement (does the internal signal cross zero at the correct confounding strength). Convincing: Spearman >= 0.5 AND the internal sign-crossing within a small tolerance of the true crossing (|delta confounding-strength| <= 0.1 of the swept range), shuffled control near 0. Refute: Spearman <= 0.2 or the signal follows the observational association (no crossing). Indeterminate band: Spearman 0.2-0.5 or crossing offset 0.1-0.25 of the range (declared before the data) -- partial fidelity, reported as qualified. A negative result means the internal signal does not track the do-calculus effect through the flip, weakening clause (b).

Experiment 4 (H3 -- steering an adjustment direction moves predictions toward the do-calculus answer): Tests clause (c).
